name: Tomas Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Dawsons at Greenway Produce, about 1,500 acres of carrots, leeks, broccoli and lettuce, nearly all of it for two big supermarket chains. Right now it's leeks and carrots, so I'm on the harvesting rig from six, or out with the weeding robots, which are little machines with cameras that pick out weeds and zap them. I'm junior, still learning the crops, and Mr Dawson's son Craig checks everything I do. In summer we've got sixty seasonal workers on the broccoli and lettuce, and I'm starting to help run a crew.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI fit into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere, honestly. I built a little app that tracks each crew's picking rate, I ask a chat app about leaf diseases when I spot something, and I watch videos from growers in other countries every night. Where I'm weak is reading the crops, the older guys can walk a field and tell you the yield, and I'm still guessing. I live with my partner Ana, she's a hairdresser, and my whole family's ten minutes away, Sunday lunch at my mum's after Mass, every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd be a let-down, if I'm honest. I think the tech is the best thing to happen to veg growing in years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who hyped it oversold it, but the tools that work are still worth having. The weeding robots save us a fortune in labour and spray. I'd keep posting about what works on our farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be disappointed, because I'd been planning my future around this. But I'd also think it's not the tech holding veg growers back, it's the supermarkets squeezing every penny and the paperwork for every worker we hire. If AI goes bust, the supermarkets are still the boss of every carrot in this field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Greenway, learn to read the crops properly from the older guys. Start growing salad on a half-acre my uncle lets me use and sell it to the restaurants in town, see if I can build something of my own. Keep saving, I've got about three months put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the boss of the carrot, the supermarket or the grower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket, every time. They tell us the size, the shape, the price, and if the carrot's bent, it goes for cattle feed. That's what gets under my skin, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why salad for restaurants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the chefs pay for quality and they don't care if it's bent. And it's mine, nobody tells me the price. It's small, but you start small.

S0.say: I'd say the people who hyped it oversold it, but the tools that work, like the weeding robots, still save a fortune in labour and spray. I'd keep posting about what works.
S0.think: I'd be disappointed because I'd planned my future around it, but the real brake on veg growers is the supermarkets' squeeze and the paperwork for hiring. The supermarkets would still be the boss of every carrot.
S0.do: Keeps working at the vegetable grower and learns to read crops from the older workers. Starts growing salad on half an acre lent by his uncle to sell to town restaurants, and keeps adding to about three months of savings.
S0.quote: If AI goes bust, the supermarkets are still the boss of every carrot in this field.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas would be disappointed by the plateau because he's betting his future on the tech. He blames supermarket power and hiring paperwork, not machines, for growers' troubles. Even in this calm scenario he'd start a small business of his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I'd bet on. And it's the one I'd want, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for growers who move fast, and that people who work hard and learn the new machines will do well. I'd say it at Mass, in the pub, anywhere. I'd also say government should keep its hands off and let farms get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's my chance to jump the queue. Right now Craig's ahead of me because he's a Dawson and he knows crops. But if the robots do the weeding and picking, the person who runs the robots matters more than the person who reads a field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the Dawsons to make me the robot lead, the person who sets up and runs the weeders and the new picking rigs. On the side, put my savings toward the deposit on a second-hand weeding robot and hire it out to smaller growers. I'd do it within six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited. Like the first day of harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the sixty seasonal workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will go, and that's hard, I know a lot of them by name. I'd be running the machine that sends half my crew home, and I'd still say it's the right call for the farm. The good ones will get trained up, I'd make sure of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't putting your savings into a robot risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But my brothers would chip in, and my dad always said you never get rich working for someone else. If it fails, I've lost a few months' savings. If it works, I've got a business.

S1.say: I'd say this is good for growers who move fast, and people who learn the machines will do well. Government should keep its hands off and let farms get on with it.
S1.think: It's my chance to jump the queue, because once robots do the weeding and picking, running them matters more than reading a field.
S1.do: Asks the owners to make him the farm's robot lead within six months. Puts savings, with help from his brothers, toward a second-hand weeding robot to hire out to smaller growers.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like the first day of harvest.
S1.quote: I'd be running the machine that sends half my crew home, and I'd still say it's the right call for the farm.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas sees steady disruption as a way to leapfrog the owner's son, and his free-market views shape a plan to own a machine and hire it out. He accepts the cost to seasonal workers openly, while promising to look after the good ones. Family money is his safety net, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then it isn't my chance any more, it's everybody's, all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, look for where you can still add something. I'd tell my family to stick together and pool what we've got. I wouldn't want the government taking over everything, but I'd admit some people would need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think in two years the big companies buy the best robots and there's no gap left for a guy like me with one second-hand weeder. Two years is too fast to borrow, build and pay it back. The big boys buy the robots and the rest of us watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not take out any loans, that'd be madness in two years. Sell the weeder idea and keep the cash. Go to the robot companies and get a job setting kit up, for as long as that lasts, and lean on family, Sunday lunches and shared bills if Ana's salon struggled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Restless, like I can't sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said keep government's hands off. Does that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, but I'm not stupid. If there's no work for anyone, someone has to keep food on the table. I'd want it to be families first, then the church, then the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger brothers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something you can sell to people who've got money, because there'll be a few with a lot. And stay close to home, because family's what's left when the job goes.

S2.say: I'd say don't panic and look for where you can still add something. My family should pool what we've got, and I'd admit some people would need government help.
S2.think: In two years the big companies buy the best robots and there's no gap for someone with one second-hand weeder. It's too fast to borrow, build and repay.
S2.do: Avoids any loans, drops the weeder business and keeps the cash. Takes a job setting up kit with a robot company while it lasts and leans on family for shared bills if his partner's salon struggles.
S2.quote: Two years is too fast to borrow, build and pay it back. The big boys buy the robots and the rest of us watch.
S2.fieldNote: Even a keen, risk-taking adopter pulls back sharply when there are only two years, because he can't finance and repay a business that fast. His views on government soften under pressure but he keeps family and church first. He sees big companies winning a fast race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something, if I start the day you tell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who start now will be fine, and the ones who wait won't. I'd say it to my brothers, my cousins, the younger lads on the crew. And I'd say rules should be simple, so a small business can buy a robot without a mountain of forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is a real window, maybe three good years of building and two of watching the big firms catch up. If I own machines and some land by year five, I'm on the right side when it lands. If I'm still a worker, I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the robot hire business in year one with my brothers, as a family firm, on top of my job at Greenway. Grow the salad half-acre into two acres. Save hard and put most of it into machines, because that's what earns when wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but buzzing. It's a race and I like races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about you working two jobs and spending the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm never home. She'd be right. Ana says I'd sell the sofa to buy a robot. She's not wrong, but I'd ask her first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you lose the race?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm a guy with a few old robots and a family who backed me. I'd still have the land, maybe, and the skills. I'd rather lose trying than wait.

S3.say: I'd say people who start now will be fine and those who wait won't. Rules should be simple enough for a small business to buy a robot without a mountain of forms.
S3.think: Five years is a real window, three good years of building and two of big firms catching up. If I own machines and some land by year five, I'm on the right side.
S3.do: Starts a family robot hire business with his brothers in year one while keeping his job. Grows his salad plot from half an acre to two acres and puts most of his savings into machines.
S3.feel: Uneasy but buzzing, like being in a race he enjoys.
S3.quote: Ana says I'd sell the sofa to buy a robot. She's not wrong, but I'd ask her first.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is long enough for Tomas to build a family business that owns machines, which he sees as the right side of the change. He frames it as a race and enjoys it. The strain on his relationship shows up in his own joke about selling the sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to own a farm. That's what I'd go for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to get ready if you're willing to work. Learn a trade, start something, stick with your family. And I'd say people should be careful about leaning on the government for everything, because it'll be tempting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see two sides. With ten years I can build a real business and maybe buy a small farm with robots doing most of the work. But the Dawsons and the big firms see it coming too, so it's a longer race with stronger runners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marry Ana, which we're planning anyway, and put off kids a couple of years while I build. Start the robot hire firm with my brothers in year one, grow it steady, and buy land around year six or seven. Do a short business course so I don't make stupid money mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It's the one where I can see a farm with my name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the crew members who lose their work, in your ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hire who I could, and teach the younger ones to run machines. Families and churches will need to step up, like they always have. I'd feel bad. I'd still buy the robot. Both are true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Across all three, what does the extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I hide my cash and grab a wage. Five, I race. Ten, I can build a farm, but so can the big boys, so it's harder than it sounds. More time helps people who'll use it, but it helps the people with money more.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty to get ready if you're willing to work: learn a trade, start something, stick with family. People should be careful not to lean on the government for everything.
S4.think: With ten years I could build a business and buy a small robot-run farm. But the big firms see it coming too, so it's a longer race with stronger runners.
S4.do: Marries his partner and delays children a couple of years while building a robot hire firm with his brothers from year one. Aims to buy land around year six or seven and takes a short business course to avoid money mistakes.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, picturing a farm with his name on it.
S4.quote: I'd feel bad. I'd still buy the robot. Both are true.
S4.fieldNote: Tomas spotted something others missed: more warning time also helps the big firms, so the race gets harder. He holds guilt and ambition side by side without resolving them. He'd delay children to build the business, a clear family trade-off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything, so the big companies just take it all and people like me end up working for them or not at all. What would help is cheap, simple loans for small growers to buy machines, and fewer forms, so a family firm can actually get started.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the supermarkets. Whatever happens with robots, they decide what a farmer earns. If they keep that power, it doesn't matter who owns the robots, they'll squeeze the price until the robot pays for them, not us.

headlineQuote: I'd feel bad. I'd still buy the robot. Both are true.
portrait: Tomas is a 27-year-old junior on a large vegetable farm supplying supermarkets, who uses AI tools every day and is starting to help run a seasonal crew. He holds traditional, free-market views, goes to Mass with his family every Sunday, and blames supermarket power and paperwork, not technology, for growers' troubles. He'd treat steady disruption as a chance to leapfrog and start a robot hire business with his brothers. Under fast AGI he'd pull back from borrowing, but with five or ten years he'd race to own machines and land. He openly holds guilt about the crew he'd replace alongside his ambition.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because there'd be no time to build a business and the big companies would take everything.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, simple loans for small growers to buy machines, and fewer forms so a family firm can get started.
